pairs.relationship: Opening address and love in truth
pairs.rationale: Both letters open with the elder addressing people loved in truth. This letter names beloved Gaius; the other names a chosen lady and her children and adds others knowing the truth. The matching address formula does not identify Gaius with another similarly named person.

pairs.relationship: Prayer for the recipient’s whole well-being
pairs.rationale: The personal prayer for health and all going well, alongside the soul's well-being, can be compared with Paul's prayer for spirit, soul and body to be kept whole. Paul's sanctification and coming context differs; neither prayer is converted into a guarantee of material prosperity.

Both report great joy over walking in truth. Here visiting brothers bear witness to the recipient's truthfulness; the other letter reports finding some of the lady's children walking in truth according to the Father's commandment. Their people and reports remain distinct.

Paul calls the recipients his glory and joy in an expectation of Jesus' coming; the elder says his greatest joy is hearing his children walk in truth. These are specific expressions of joy in the recipients, without identifying the groups or turning children into an asserted biological relationship.

The faithful action toward brothers who are strangers provides a concrete counterpart to Hebrews' command not to forget hospitality. Hebrews adds unknowingly entertaining angels; this letter calls the welcomed people brothers and does not identify them as angels.

The request to send the brothers onward worthily corresponds to the instruction to send Zenas and Apollos onward diligently so they lack nothing. The named travelers and practical supply instruction in Titus are a comparison, not an identification of the unnamed brothers here.

Paul describes proclaiming the good news without charge so as not to make full use of his right in it. This gives a concrete mission-and-payment comparison with travelers receiving nothing from the Gentiles for the Name's sake; the different recipients and scope of payment restraint remain distinct.

The Philippians' sharing in affliction and sending supplies for Paul's need gives a concrete example of support for gospel work. Here the obligation to support such travelers makes supporters fellow workers with the truth; this letter does not name the Philippians or specify the same gifts.

pairs.relationship: Loving first place and servant leadership
pairs.rationale: Diotrephes' love of being first and refusal to welcome the writer can be set beside Jesus' contrast between domineering rulers and becoming first through service as slave of all. This is a specific leadership contrast, not an assertion that Diotrephes was among the Gospel's hearers.

The earlier commendation of faithful welcome and instruction to support traveling brothers directly contrasts with refusing brothers, obstructing willing hosts and expelling them here. The letter itself supplies the opposed conduct; no unprinted details about the expulsion's procedure are added.

Both statements distinguish a relation to God by conduct. First John names not practicing righteousness and not loving a brother; this letter contrasts doing good as from God with doing evil and not seeing God. The predicates are related without being exchanged as identical clauses.

The Gospel's statement that we know the disciple's testimony is true provides a specific testimony-assurance counterpart to we also bear witness and you know our testimony is true. The different witnesses and Demetrius' commendation remain distinct; the link does not identify him as that disciple.

pairs.relationship: Writing materials and a desired visit
pairs.rationale: Both closings set many things to write beside a preference for personal communication. Second John names paper and ink; this verse names ink and a reed pen, with the face-to-face hope following separately in native verse14. Their native divisions and material words remain intact.

Both letters hope for personal presence and speaking face to face. Here the writer hopes to see the recipient soon; Second John hopes to come and adds the purpose of completed joy and a writing-material contrast. The different verbs and clauses do not establish the same planned journey.

pairs.relationship: Greeting and a wish of peace
pairs.rationale: Both closings join mutual greeting with a wish of peace. Peter names a kiss of love and all who are in Christ; this letter exchanges friends' greetings and asks greeting by name. Neither closing supplies the other's addressees or manner as unprinted words.
